messages.content: Write the opening section of a blog post explaining why observability matters for engineering teams. Around 250 words.

output:
Clean through the slopwatch gate. Here's the opening (~250 words):

---

## Your dashboards are lying to you

At 2:14 a.m. the pager goes off. CPU is fine. Memory is fine. Five green dashboards insist the system is healthy, and meanwhile checkout is failing for something like three percent of users, and nobody on the call can say which three percent, or why.

That gap between "all systems nominal" and "the thing is broken" is the whole reason observability exists. Monitoring answers questions you were smart enough to ask in advance. Observability lets you ask new ones at 2:14 a.m., against data you already have, without shipping a build first.

The distinction sounds academic right up until you're the one on the call. Monitoring tells you p99 latency crossed 800ms. An observable system tells you it crossed 800ms only for requests carrying a particular feature flag, from one region, routed to a read replica that fell twenty minutes behind sometime around the last deploy. One of those is a fact. The other is an answer.

Most teams get to the second kind the expensive way: an outage, a week of postmortem, a resolution to "add more logging next time." Then the next incident arrives wearing a different mask, the logs are the wrong logs, and the cycle repeats. What breaks isn't the software. It's the team's ability to reason about the software it already shipped.

This post is about closing that gap on purpose, before the pager makes the decision for you.

---

The 800ms / three percent / twenty minutes numbers are placeholders — swap in real figures from one of your own incidents and the section gets noticeably sharper.
